catalog_quote: The syllable is defined as the rank whose units have a structure in terms of phonemes and which functions in the rhythm group. The rhythm group consists of one to three syllables; only the last is stressed. The bulk of the language corpus consists of rhythm groups with only one syllable. The focus of this study is therefore on the more complex stressed syllable. The core of the stressed syllable includes a consonantal margin, a vocalic nucleus and a tonal prosody. A minimal syllable includes a consonant (C) or a laryngeal (L), one vowel (V) and one tone (T). The maximum expansion of the syllable includes a cluster of a laryngeal, a consonant and a semivowel (S); a vowel cluster, a glottal closure (ʔ), nasalization (N) and two tones or one tone and ballistic stress (´).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tone language (four level tones plus three contour sequences, and a ballistic/controlled syllable contrast). The phonological word ('rhythm group') is one to three syllables long and stress falls on its last syllable; any preceding syllables are unstressed pretonic syllables with reduced segmental and tonal inventories. Most words are monosyllabic. Corroborated independently by Lewis & Rensch 1971 ms. sec.7: the core of the phonological word is the stressed syllable, optionally preceded by 'one or rarely two pretonic syllables'; ballistic accent occurs only in the stressed syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: None. (Spanish loans such as /ka4hwi1/ 'cow', /pi lai/ 'Felipe' are cited with the same pretonic + stressed-final shape.) The contrastive 'ballistic stress/accent' marked with an acute is a syllable-type feature of the stressed syllable, not a competing stress position.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is Thelin's 'rhythm group' = Lewis & Rensch's 'phonological word' (root syllable plus up to two prefixal/pretonic syllables); statements are about word-level forms in isolation and in text, not phrase-level prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: Both primary sources describe the Chinantec of San Juan Bautista Tlacoatzintepec (Cuicatlan district, Oaxaca) = Glottolog tlac1239 / ISO ctl exactly; Thelin notes the same variety is spoken in surrounding hamlets and by migrants in Chiltepec, with minor phonological differences among the town's three barrios. No dialect mismatch.

new_statements.quote: p.88: "En chinanteco las palabras que se pronuncian con más fuerza se escriben con acento. Fíjate en los siguientes pares de palabras. Las dos palabras de cada par llevan el mismo tono, pero la segunda se escribe con acento porque se pronuncia con más fuerza. jan pluma / ján espuma; ñin sal / ñín nueve; kin seco / kín cuatro; jain lodo / jáin cama" — p.146: "En estas palabras la primera sílaba lleva tono bajo con acento: ÚGuun Quetzalapa; mánminh poco a poco; kiákio diecisiete; ÚTá Cuicatlán" — p.8: "Existen cuatro tonos básicos: el tono más alto, el tono alto, el tono medio y el tono bajo."
new_statements.translation: p.88: "In Chinantec the words that are pronounced with more force are written with an accent. Look at the following pairs of words. Both words of each pair carry the same tone, but the second is written with an accent because it is pronounced with more force. jan feather / ján foam; ñin salt / ñín nine; kin dry / kín four; jain mud / jáin bed" — p.146: "In these words the first syllable carries low tone with accent: ÚGuun Quetzalapa; mánminh little by little; kiákio seventeen; ÚTá Cuicatlán" — p.8: "There are four basic tones: the highest tone, the high tone, the mid tone and the low tone."

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's 'tone language with a stress statement' record (Thelin 1980: rhythm group of 1-3 syllables, only the last stressed). The primer adds no placement statement; it corroborates the four-tone system and the ballistic ('more force') lexical accent that Thelin and Lewis & Rensch describe, and shows accent-marked initial syllables in a few disyllabic compound-like forms (p.146). Given Lewis & Rensch's 'the ballistic accent does not occur in unstressed syllables', those forms are most simply two rhythm groups (e.g. Ú- 'town' + name; 'ten'+'seven'), so they do not contradict final stress within the rhythm group, but the primer itself does not say so. Caveat: the text rea…
new_statements.rule_in_words: A Spanish-to-Chinantec transition primer, not a grammar. It says the language is tonal (four basic tones, p.8) and that some words are 'pronounced with more force' and are therefore written with an acute accent, contrasting with same-tone words without it (jan/ján etc.). That 'acento' is the lexical ballistic-vs-controlled syllable contrast (what Thelin 1980 calls 'ballistic stress' and Lewis & Rensch 1971 the 'ballistic accent'), a property of individual words, not a positional word-stress rule. The primer never says which syllable of a polysyllabic word carries stress; the p.146 list shows the accent written on the first syllable of some two-syllable items (place names with Ú-, the numeral kiákio 'seventeen', mánminh 'little by little'), which are compound-like forms.
new_statements.exceptions: None on stress placement. Lecciones 34-35, 40, 42 (pp.234, 241, 274, 286) add that h-final words (glottal/checked syllables) can also carry the accent, and p.241 says all mid-tone h-final words carry the accent ('Todas las palabras que llevan tono medio y terminan con h llevan acento, porque todas se pronuncian con más fuerza').
new_statements.identity_note: The primer is explicitly for 'chinanteco de Tlacoatzintepec' (San Juan Bautista Tlacoatzintepec, Oaxaca); its collaborators are residents of that town. Same variety as the catalog entry and as Thelin 1980 / Lewis & Rensch 1971.

sources.note: p.1 Introduction: 'The rhythm group consists of one to three syllables; only the last is stressed. The bulk of the language corpus consists of rhythm groups with only one syllable.' Sec.3 'The prosody' (pp.5-6): syllables are ballistic (acute accent) or controlled; four level tones (1 very high.. 4 low) plus sequences 12, 34, 42; 'two tones or one tone and ballistic stress' in the maximal syllable; /r/ is an affricate in stressed syllables, a flap in unstressed syllables (p.2).
